opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to recognize is that background work in agents is really a distributed systems problem wearing a new costume. When an agent kicks off something long-running, like a big refactor, a research task, or a multi-step workflow that touches a bunch of external APIs, you've suddenly got all the classic problems: durability, retries, idempotency, observability, and what happens when something fails halfway through.

The way I tend to think about it is in three layers. At the bottom you need durable execution. The agent's state, meaning the conversation, the plan, the intermediate tool results, has to be checkpointed somewhere so that if a process dies or a container gets preempted, you resume rather than restart. Workflow engines and durable execution frameworks have been doing this for years, and I think agent builders are rediscovering why they matter. An LLM call is expensive and nondeterministic, so replaying from scratch isn't just slow, it can give you a different trajectory entirely.

The middle layer is scheduling and isolation. Background agents need sandboxes, and they need resource limits, both compute and spend. You don't want a runaway loop burning tokens at 3am with nobody watching. So you want budgets, timeouts, and some notion of priority, the same way you'd treat batch jobs in a cluster.

The top layer, which I think is the most underexplored, is the human interface. How does background work surface back to the person? If the agent hits an ambiguous decision, does it block and ask, make a reversible choice and flag it, or pick the conservative path? The best systems make work inspectable and interruptible, so you can check in, see a legible summary of what's happened, redirect, and let it continue. That's less a backend problem and more a product and trust problem.

And one point people underweight: the boundary between foreground and background should be fluid. You start something interactively, realize it'll take a while, push it to the background, and later pull it forward again. Making that handoff seamless, with no lost context and no duplicated side effects, is where a lot of the real engineering goes.

r001.rationale: The response discusses surfacing background work to a person and resuming or redirecting it, but does not say that task completion triggers a signal that wakes the agent.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that background work is really the thing that separates a chatbot from an agent. A chatbot is request-response. You ask, it answers, the turn ends. An agent has to keep doing things when nobody's looking, and that changes the architecture pretty fundamentally.

The first thing you run into is that the model call is no longer the unit of work. The unit of work is a task, and a task might span dozens of model calls, tool calls, waits on external systems, maybe a human approval in the middle. So you need something that owns that task's lifecycle independently of any single request. In practice that looks a lot like a durable workflow engine. You want the state checkpointed, you want to be able to resume after a crash, and you want retries to be idempotent, because the model will happily call the same tool twice if you replay a step naively.

The second thing is that you have to be really deliberate about the boundary between the foreground conversation and the background jobs. The user is still talking to the agent while stuff is running. So you need a clean way for background tasks to surface results back into the conversation, and for the user to interrupt or redirect them. I think of it almost like an event bus. Tasks emit progress and completion events, the foreground loop subscribes, and the model gets to decide when and how to tell the user. If you just dump raw tool output into the context every time something finishes, you blow up the context and you confuse the model.

Third is isolation. Background work is where the risky stuff happens, because by definition the human isn't watching. So each task should run in its own sandbox with its own scoped credentials, and the permissions a user granted for one step shouldn't silently carry over to a different task that spins up later. That's partly a safety thing and partly just good hygiene, because it makes the blast radius of a bad action small and debuggable.

And then the last piece, which people underestimate, is observability. When something goes wrong in a thirty-step background job, you need to be able to see the whole trace, what the model saw at each step, what it decided, what the tool returned. Without that you're basically debugging with print statements inside a black box. So I'd say the stack is: durable task state, an event-driven bridge back to the conversation, strong isolation per task, and traces as a first-class artifact. If you get those four right, the model is honestly the easy part.

r001.rationale: The candidate says tasks emit completion events and the foreground loop subscribes to them, communicating a completion signal that can notify or wake the agent.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to separate the agent’s reasoning loop from the lifetime of the work it kicks off. If a task takes ten minutes, you don’t want the whole interaction sitting there waiting on a tool call. You want to start the work, get back a handle, and let the agent continue—or let the user come back later.

That means making the work durable: tracking its state, persisting its results, and having a way to notify the agent when something changes. Then you have to decide what that notification actually does. Does it wake the agent up? Does it wait until the next user interaction? Does it require a decision before anything else happens?

And a lot of the hard parts are distributed systems problems. What happens if the worker crashes? Can you retry without sending the same email twice? What happens if the user changes their mind while the task is running? I’d put those guarantees in the surrounding system, so the model can focus on deciding what work to do and interpreting the result.

r001.rationale: The response mentions notifying the agent and asks whether a notification should wake it, but does not affirm that background-task completion can trigger a wake-up signal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between the agent deciding what work needs to happen and the system making sure that work actually happens. You don’t want a long-running task to depend on one model call or one process staying alive.

So I’d put durable execution underneath the agent: persist the task, enqueue the work, and let workers pick it up. Then make the lifecycle explicit—what’s running, what’s waiting on something, what failed, and what needs a human decision. If a worker dies, you should be able to resume without asking the model to reconstruct everything.

The tricky part is side effects. Retrying a reasoning step is one thing; retrying a step that sends an email or charges a card is another. You need idempotency and clear boundaries around those actions.

And then there’s the interaction layer. If an agent says, “I’ll work on this in the background,” that’s a promise. The architecture needs to support progress updates, cancellation, and getting the result back to the user. A queue alone doesn’t give you that.

r001.rationale: The response describes workers picking up queued work and returning results to the user, but does not say that task completion sends a signal that wakes the agent.
